Some will say, "Slavery was a long time ago." So let me bring us forward.

Reconstruction was drowned in the blood of Black citizens, as the federal government withdrew its protections and allowed white supremacist terror to reign across the South.

Jim Crow was not merely Southern custom—it was law, enforced by police, upheld by courts, and tolerated by the federal government for nearly a century.

The New Deal—perhaps the greatest expansion of the American middle class in history—was deliberately structured to exclude Black Americans. Social Security initially excluded domestic workers and agricultural laborers. The Federal Housing Administration didn't just fail to help Black families—it drew the red lines on the maps itself, marking Black neighborhoods as unworthy of investment. The GI Bill, which built white suburban America, was administered in ways that systematically denied Black veterans the same benefits.

These were not ancient sins. There are people alive today who were denied FHA loans. There are people alive today who were turned away from universities their tax dollars funded. There are people alive today who drank from separate fountains, attended underfunded schools, and were beaten for the crime of trying to vote.

And let us be unflinching about the economics. Economists have estimated that the value of slave labor alone—unpaid wages, exposed to compound interest—amounts to trillions of dollars. Add to that the wealth stolen through sharecropping, convict leasing, redlining, predatory lending, discriminatory hiring, and mass incarceration, and we are talking about the largest sustained theft of labor and wealth in human history.

Today, the median white family holds roughly eight times the wealth of the median Black family. That gap is not an accident. It is the mathematically predictable result of centuries of policy.

Why Direct Financial Reparations

Now—some people of goodwill say, "I support addressing racism, but why direct payments? Why not invest in communities, in education, in programs?"

I'll tell you why.

First, because we have tried the indirect approach, and the wealth gap has barely moved. We have had civil rights legislation for sixty years, and yet the gap between Black and white wealth is roughly the same as it was in 1968. Programs can be defunded. Initiatives can be quietly gutted. But a check that has been cashed is a fact that cannot be undone.

Second, because direct payment is what justice looks like. When Japanese Americans were interned, we did not offer them a scholarship program. We offered them direct payments and a formal apology. When we have wrongfully convicted individuals, we do not offer them job training—we offer them compensation. The principle is elementary: when you have taken something from someone, you give it back. You don't get to choose a more convenient form of restitution.

Third, because wealth is freedom in America. Wealth is the down payment on a home. Wealth is the ability to start a business, to weather an emergency, to send your child to college, to leave an inheritance. To deny that Black Americans were systematically robbed of the ability to build wealth, and then to deny them the most direct means of addressing that robbery, is to perpetuate the very injustice we claim to oppose.

I know the objections. Let me meet them head-on.

"I never owned slaves." No, you didn't. But you inherited a country whose wealth, institutions, and infrastructure were built on slave labor. Reparations are not about personal guilt. They are about national responsibility. The United States government committed these acts, and the United States government endures. We pay debts incurred by previous Congresses every single day. This debt is no different—except that we have ignored it far longer.

"It's too complicated to implement." We have the IRS. We have the Census Bureau. We have genealogical records. We have sent stimulus checks to hundreds of millions of Americans in a matter of weeks. If the will exists, the mechanism will follow. HR 40, the bill to simply study reparations, languished in Congress for over thirty years. We cannot even muster the courage to study the question? That is not a logistical objection—it is a moral failure.

"It will be divisive." The division already exists. It exists in every metric of American life—life expectancy, maternal mortality, incarceration rates, household wealth, homeownership, exposure to environmental toxins. The division was created by policy, and it can only be healed by policy. What is truly divisive is asking Black Americans to accept permanent disadvantage and call it equality.

"Where does it end?" It ends where justice begins. It ends when we have made a serious, tangible, good-faith effort to repair what was broken. No one asks this question when we spend trillions on defense, or when we bail out banks, or when we subsidize corporations. Only when the beneficiaries are Black Americans does the nation suddenly discover fiscal restraint.

Let me close with this.

America loves to call itself the greatest nation on Earth. We inscribe "justice" on our courthouses and "liberty" on our coins. We tell ourselves a story about a country founded on the proposition that all men are created equal.

But a nation that steals two and a half centuries of labor and then tells the descendants of that theft to simply "work harder"—that nation has not yet reckoned with its own story.

A nation that systematically strips wealth from a people for generations, that builds its middle class on policies designed to exclude them, and then marvels at the "achievement gap"—that nation is engaged not in ignorance but in willful denial.

Reparations are not charity. They are not a handout. They are not an act of white guilt or liberal overreach. They are the settlement of a debt. A debt documented in ship manifests and auction records. A debt recorded in redlining maps and court decisions. A debt written into the very soil of this country, which was cleared, planted, and harvested by people who never saw a dime for their labor.

We are often told that America is a nation of laws. Then let us follow the most basic principle of law: when you have been unjustly enriched at another's expense, you owe restitution.

Frederick Douglass once said, "Power concedes nothing without a demand." Black Americans have been demanding justice since the first enslaved person set foot on this continent. The question is not whether the demand is legitimate. It is whether this generation of Americans will finally have the decency to answer it.

Let us be that generation.

Let us pay the debt.

Let us, at long last, put our money where our mouth is—and prove that when we say "liberty and justice for all," we mean all.
